blocks.text: One reading of verses 1–17 understands the warning against seeking Egypt’s protection and relying on swift horses within an Assyrian-era setting. On this reading, the chapter treats foreign alliances and military resources not as merely political choices, but as expressions of where Judah places its trust. The contrast in verse 15—strength in returning, rest, quietness, and confidence—therefore addresses the same crisis from a different direction.

The Great Isaiah Scroll is an almost complete witness to all sixty-six chapters of Isaiah. It broadly aligns with the Masoretic tradition while also containing thousands of spelling and substantive differences; other Isaiah manuscripts and interpretive writings from Qumran likewise reflect active copying and interpretation of the book. This provides a wider textual setting for reading Isaiah 30, though it does not itself settle how any individual verse should be understood.
